title: Node isolation and rolling throttle playbook
content:
Context and intent:
This is a working playbook for handling node isolation scenarios and controlled rolling upgrades on on-prem Kubernetes clusters (bare metal and vSphere). It focuses on minimizing SLO impact during maintenance, mitigating noisy-neighbor eviction storms, and coordinating Terraform-driven infra changes with cluster lifecycle operations.

Audience:
Primarily SREs and field-deploy engineers running Redwood Private clusters. Also useful to solutions engineering when planning customer handoffs.

High-level goals:
- Provide a low-risk, observable sequence for cluster control-plane and worker node changes.
- Define throttles and isolation knobs to avoid mass evictions during network flaps, IPMI storms, or power events.
- Capture Terraform module notes so infra changes (NIC replacements, vSphere VM resize, BMC reboots) can be paired safely with in-cluster actions (drain, kubelet-cordon, K8s upgrade).

Quick summary checklist (pre-run):
- Verify prometheus and alertmanager silence windows are set for the maintenance window.
- Confirm kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, API server availability >= 2/3 control plane quorum (for HA clusters).
- Export kubeconfig and validate kubectl connectivity from a bastion.
- Take etcd snapshot and copy to secure object storage (s3://private-backups/customer-x/).
- Lock Terraform plan approvals (prevent concurrent infra changes).

Common isolation scenarios and mitigation patterns:
1) Partial network segment flaps (top-of-rack switch):
  - Symptoms: Several nodes show transient NotReady, kube-proxy evictions, packet loss to control plane.
  - Immediate action: Increase pod-eviction-timeout temporarily via the kubelet flag and node annotation: "node.alpha.kubernetes.io/eviction-timeout": "10m"
  - Use a rolling check: name nodes impacted, do not mass-drain. For each affected node: kubectl cordon <node>; attempt gentle restart of network services; if recoverable within 5m, uncordon.

2) vSphere host maintenance (planned host patching):
  - Prework: set vSphere maintenance mode for the ESXi host; identify VMs (control plane or worker) that will be moved/evacuated.
  - For control plane VMs: prefer live migration (vMotion). If eviction is required, do stepwise evictions and ensure etcd member removal/add flows are tested.
  - For workers: use controlled drain with timeout and PDB awareness: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=30m

3) BMC/IPMI-provisioner mass reboots (factory reimage):
  - Avoid simultaneous BMC-triggered reboots across >N/3 of nodes for HA clusters.
  - Recommended throttle: 3 nodes max concurrently for clusters <= 15 nodes; 10% of fleet (rounded up) for larger clusters.

Terraform module notes (practical knobs):
- Module: onprem/node (variables):
  - "node_reboot_window_minutes": default 20, used by orchestration to pace BMC reboots.
  - "maintenance_label": applied to VMs so k8s can auto-select maintenance candidates.
  - "drain_policy": choices=[immediate, staged, off] — default staged. When set to staged, infra pipeline will pause until a readiness-check webhook returns success.
- Module: vsphere/control_plane (notes):
  - Expose an input to gate upgrades: "api_server_max_unavailable" – Terraform will annotate the cluster upgrade Job to limit concurrent control-plane restarts.
- Recommended output from infra plan: list of affected node hostnames and a simple CSV: name, ip, role, expected-downtime-mins — pipe this into the runbook step.

Orchestration patterns (preferred):
- Layer 0 (infrastructure): run Terraform plan -> apply with "maintenance" label on target VMs.
- Layer 1 (coordination): invoke k8s-side agent (or GitHub Actions runner) that performs drained nodes in the same maintenance group. Agent implements pacing from module variable.
- Layer 2 (verification): smoke test control plane (kubectl get nodes; run a small canary job) -> run metrics regression test (latency, error-rate).

Rolling throttle design (concrete knobs):
- Worker throttle controller (example heuristics):
  - max_concurrent_drains = ceil(min(0.1 * total_workers, 5))
  - inter_drain_delay = configurable, default 90s
  - per-node drain timeout = 30m
- Control plane throttle (HA clusters):
  - allow one control-plane restart at a time in 3+ control-plane clusters. For 5-node cp, allow at most 2 simultaneous restarts but staged with quorum check between each.

Kubernetes-side helpers (practical commands & scripts):
- drain-with-pdb-check.sh (rough):
  - for node in list:
      if check-pods-respect-pdb(node) then kubectl drain node --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=1800s else schedule delayed retry
- quick-health-checks after node rejoin:
  - wait-for-ready pods on node (label selector)
  - run kube-bench quick checks for kubelet connectivity

Upgrade plan sketch (control-plane + kubelet):
1) Take etcd snapshot; store offbox.
2) Verify cluster state (no pending critical upgrades, no failing core pods).
3) Run upgrade on a single control-plane node following: cordon -> drain non-critical pods -> apt/yum upgrade + kubeadm upgrade apply (if applicable) -> restart kubelet -> uncordon -> verify control-plane components healthy.
4) Wait 10–15 minutes (observability) and run acceptance tests (API latency, etcd ops per sec).
5) Proceed to next control-plane node, but reduce concurrency if any regressions observed.
6) Worker kubelet upgrades: use drain policy with max_concurrent_drains defined earlier.

Rollback and emergency stop guidance:
- If etcd latency or quorum drops, STOP the playbook and initiate rollback: restore etcd from latest snapshot to a temporary restore cluster to validate.
- If mass eviction detected (more nodes NotReady than expected), cancel ongoing infra changes and start rejoin attempts using kubelet restart + ip route reset.

Observability & safety nets:
- Important metrics to watch during run:
  - API server 95th/99th latency
  - etcd commit duration & leader changes
  - node kubelet ready counts and pod evictions per minute
- Dashboards: maintenance-mode panel (shows nodes in maintenance label), eviction storm alert, etcd-quorum-loss alert.

Field notes / recent gotchas (collected):
- vSphere SR-IOV NIC passthrough VMs losing VF assignments after vMotion; solution: mark these VMs as non-migratable and schedule host patching accordingly.
- PXE/iPXE stacks: careful ordering of DHCP (avoid duplicate DHCP servers in the same VLAN).
- On older BMC firmware, power cycles can leave NIC in weird state; always validate NIC link after BMC cycle before uncordoning.

To-dos / follow-ups:
- Add a small operator to enforce rolling throttle via CRD (proto: RollingThrottle with group config in infra module).
- Author a Terraform plan wrapper that outputs a structured maintenance CSV consumed by the runbook agent.
- Document a minimal test harness for smoke-testing cluster behavior during partial-power events.

Appendix: useful commands (cheat sheet)
- etcd snapshot: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=$EP snapshot save /tmp/snap.db
- restore: etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/snap.db
- cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
- drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=1800s
- uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>

Notes to self: keep this doc terse — more procedural checklists should be split per-customer (templates). Link the maintenance CSV to the deploy pipeline so operators don't have to hand-type hostnames.

Contact: Ava Patel (eng-private-deployments) — reach via slack #private-deployments or DM for runbook dry-runs.
